animals.viewing_tips: Visit vegetated pond margins and slow stream sections on rainy or overcast days in winter. Look for reddish hind legs beneath the water surface and listen for their soft, low grunting calls — quiet approach is essential as this federally threatened species is wary.

animals.name: Wood Frog
animals.behavior_notes: Wood Frogs are among the earliest spring breeders, emerging from frozen leaf litter to call and mate explosively in vernal pools often while snow is still on the ground. Their quacking duck-like chorus can be heard from a considerable distance on warm, rainy evenings.
animals.viewing_tips: Locate vernal pools in deciduous forest during the first warm rains of late winter and listen for their distinctive duck-like quacking calls. Breeding congregations can be very dense and are easy to observe — this explosive breeding event lasts only a week or two.

animals.name: American Toad
animals.behavior_notes: American Toads breed in spring from April through June, with males producing long, melodious trilling calls from shallow ponds and stream edges. Outside of breeding season they are terrestrial insectivores found in gardens, forests, and fields.
animals.viewing_tips: Listen for their sustained musical trill near any shallow pond or wetland edge on warm spring evenings. They are extremely common and approachable — breeding choruses can be deafening and males are easy to spot at the water's edge calling in full view.

animals.name: Spotted Salamander
animals.behavior_notes: Spotted Salamanders emerge on the first warm rainy nights of late winter — often called 'Big Night' — migrating en masse to vernal pools to breed. After a few frenzied nights of breeding, they return underground and are rarely seen again until the following year.
animals.viewing_tips: Monitor vernal pools in deciduous forest on the first nights when temperatures exceed 40°F and rain is falling in late February or March. Visit pools with a red-filtered flashlight to observe breeding aggregations without disturbing them — this single annual event is spectacular.

animals.name: Axolotl
parks: Xochimilco Ecological Park (no established US NP population)
animals.behavior_notes: Axolotls are critically endangered and native to the lake complex of Xochimilco near Mexico City. They do not exist in any established wild population within the United States.
animals.viewing_tips: Axolotls have no wild US population and are effectively extinct in the wild globally. They can be seen in captivity at select US aquariums such as the Shedd Aquarium in Chicago, IL.

animals.name: Spring Peeper
animals.behavior_notes: Spring Peepers emerge from leaf litter shortly after ice thaws, often beginning to call on the first warm rainy nights of late winter or early spring. Males gather in large choruses near ponds, swamps, and woodland pools to attract mates.
animals.viewing_tips: Visit slow-moving or still bodies of water at dusk during the first warm evenings above 40°F after rain. Listen for their iconic high-pitched peeping calls — though heard easily, spotting individuals requires patience and a flashlight to scan vegetation near the water's edge.

animals.name: Atlantic Salmon
animals.behavior_notes: Atlantic Salmon return to natal rivers in fall to spawn, making them visible as they leap upstream through rapids and fish ladders. Their numbers in the US are critically low, concentrated in a handful of Maine rivers.
animals.viewing_tips: Visit the Narraguagus or Penobscot River in Maine during October spawning runs; check with local fish ladders such as the one at Veazie for best viewing access.

animals.name: Chinook Salmon
animals.behavior_notes: Chinook Salmon, the largest Pacific salmon species, make dramatic upstream spawning runs in fall, often visible in clear shallow rivers as they push against currents. Males develop hooked jaws and deep red coloration during spawning.
animals.viewing_tips: The Hoh and Queets Rivers in Olympic National Park offer excellent viewing of fall Chinook runs; polarized sunglasses help you spot fish through the water surface.

animals.name: Sockeye Salmon
animals.behavior_notes: Sockeye Salmon turn brilliant red with green heads during their spawning run, making them one of the most visually striking salmon species to observe. They congregate in massive numbers at Brooks Falls in Katmai, attracting bears and providing world-class wildlife viewing.
animals.viewing_tips: Brooks Falls in Katmai NP is the premier viewing location; secure a spot at the viewing platform early as access is limited and permits are required during peak season.

animals.name: Coho Salmon
animals.behavior_notes: Coho Salmon enter freshwater streams in fall and are known for their acrobatic leaping behavior at obstacles. They prefer smaller coastal streams and are often seen in forest-lined rivers where they spawn under overhanging vegetation.
animals.viewing_tips: Look for Coho in the Sol Duc and Elwha Rivers within Olympic National Park; wearing waders and approaching quietly from downstream gives the best viewing angles without disturbing spawning fish.

animals.name: Steelhead Trout
animals.behavior_notes: Steelhead Trout are sea-run rainbow trout that return to coastal rivers in winter, displaying powerful upstream swimming behavior. Unlike Pacific salmon, steelhead can survive spawning and return to the ocean, making repeated runs possible.
animals.viewing_tips: The Smith River near Redwood National Park is a premier steelhead viewing river; visit during winter rain events when river levels rise slightly, as fish move upstream with fresh pulses of water.

animals.name: Lake Sturgeon
animals.behavior_notes: Lake Sturgeon gather at spawning shoals in May and June, rolling and splashing conspicuously at the surface in shallow rocky areas of rivers and lake margins. These ancient fish can exceed 100 years in age and 200 pounds in weight.
animals.viewing_tips: The Sturgeon spawning runs on the Bois Brule River in Wisconsin and at Black Lake, Michigan are well-documented public viewing events; arrive at dusk near rocky shoals for best sightings.

animals.name: White Sturgeon
parks: Columbia River Gorge National Scenic Area
animals.behavior_notes: White Sturgeon, North America's largest freshwater fish, are sometimes seen rolling or jumping near the surface in the Columbia and Snake Rivers during spring. They congregate below dams and in deep river pools where currents slow.
animals.viewing_tips: Bonneville Dam on the Columbia River has underwater viewing windows where White Sturgeon are regularly visible; the adjacent hatchery also keeps display sturgeon for guaranteed sightings.

animals.name: Paddlefish
animals.behavior_notes: Paddlefish move into shallow backwaters and tributary mouths in early spring to spawn, and are occasionally spotted near the surface in calm pools with their distinctive paddle-shaped rostrum visible. They filter-feed on zooplankton by swimming with mouths agape.
animals.viewing_tips: Visit the confluence areas of the Missouri and Yellowstone Rivers in Montana or Lake Texoma on the Oklahoma-Texas border during spring; look for their rostrum breaking the surface in calm stretches of large rivers.

animals.name: Alligator Gar
animals.behavior_notes: Alligator Gar are often seen rolling at the surface to gulp air using their swim bladder as a supplemental lung during warm summer months. They congregate in slow-moving backwaters, bayous, and oxbow lakes where they ambush prey near cover.
animals.viewing_tips: Paddle quietly through backwater sloughs in Big Thicket National Preserve or Trinity River NWR in Texas at dawn; look for their distinctive broad snout breaking the surface as they roll to breathe.

animals.name: Manta Ray
animals.behavior_notes: Oceanic Manta Rays occasionally visit warm Florida and Hawaii waters in summer, performing spectacular barrel rolls near the surface as they feed on plankton concentrations. They are drawn to upwellings and tidal currents that concentrate their zooplankton prey.
animals.viewing_tips: Snorkel or dive the outer reef areas of Biscayne National Park or join a sanctioned dive tour off Kona, Hawaii during summer; look for their wingtips breaking the surface near plankton-rich upwelling areas.

animals.name: Whale Shark
animals.behavior_notes: Whale sharks aggregate in warm Gulf Stream waters during summer months, often feeding near the surface on plankton blooms and fish spawn. They are slow-moving filter feeders and are generally tolerant of snorkelers and divers.
animals.viewing_tips: Book a dive charter out of Key West or Islamorada that specializes in pelagic encounters; encounters are opportunistic and not guaranteed. Scanning the surface from the bow of a boat for their distinctive dorsal fin and spotted pattern is the best detection method.

animals.name: Hammerhead Shark
animals.behavior_notes: Scalloped hammerheads move inshore along Florida coastal waters during summer, often hunting rays and fish in shallow reef zones at dawn and dusk. They are generally shy around divers but can be spotted patrolling reef edges.
animals.viewing_tips: Diving or snorkeling the outer reefs of Biscayne National Park offers the best chance of sighting; go early morning before boat traffic increases. Joining a guided reef dive with a local operator increases odds significantly.

animals.name: Great White Shark
animals.behavior_notes: Great white sharks aggregate around the Channel Islands and nearby Farallon Islands in fall and winter to prey on pinnipeds such as sea lions and elephant seals. They are most active near seal haul-out sites during morning hours.
animals.viewing_tips: Cage diving and shark watching tours depart from San Diego and other Southern California ports; the Farallon Islands off San Francisco also offer world-class surface sightings from permitted research vessels. Observe from a boat — in-water encounters are extremely dangerous.

animals.name: Bull Shark
animals.behavior_notes: Bull sharks are uniquely tolerant of fresh and brackish water and are commonly found in the estuaries and river mouths of the Everglades during warmer months. They are highly opportunistic predators and most active near dawn and dusk.
animals.viewing_tips: Airboat and kayak tours through the Everglades mangrove estuaries occasionally spot bull sharks near the Ten Thousand Islands area; observe only from watercraft and never wade or swim in murky estuary waters. A licensed guide familiar with local waterways greatly improves sighting chances.

animals.name: Coelacanth
parks: N/A — No US national park habitat
animals.behavior_notes: The coelacanth is a critically endangered living fossil found only in deep ocean waters off the coasts of East Africa and Indonesia — it does not occur in wild US waters. It is a nocturnal, deep-water species that rests in underwater caves during the day.
animals.viewing_tips: Coelacanths cannot be viewed in the wild in the United States; they do not exist in US waters. The closest viewing opportunity for US residents is at certain public aquariums or natural history museum exhibits featuring preserved specimens — no wild viewing is possible domestically.

animals.name: Brook Trout
animals.behavior_notes: Brook trout are most active and visible in cold, clear mountain streams during spring and fall when water temperatures are ideal and insect hatches are abundant. In October they enter spawning season, moving into shallow gravel riffles where their vivid colors are easiest to spot.
animals.viewing_tips: Wade slowly and quietly into cold headwater streams in Shenandoah's backcountry — polarized sunglasses are essential for spotting brook trout holding in current seams and behind rocks. Early morning before midday light creates glare is the optimal observation window.

animals.name: Largemouth Bass
animals.behavior_notes: Largemouth bass are highly active during spring when warming water temperatures trigger pre-spawn and spawn behavior, making them aggressive and visible in shallow vegetated areas. They patrol lily pads, submerged logs, and reed edges at dawn and dusk hunting prey.
animals.viewing_tips: Canoe or kayak slowly along the edges of oxbow lakes and slow-moving bayous in Big Thicket Preserve at first light; look for bass cruising or hovering motionless near submerged structure in clear shallows. Polarized sunglasses dramatically improve visibility into the water column.

animals.name: Monarch Butterfly
animals.behavior_notes: Monarchs gather in large roosts and nectaring clusters during fall migration, fueling up on milkweed and wildflowers before heading to overwintering grounds in Mexico. Warm, sunny midday hours prompt the most active flight and feeding behavior.
animals.viewing_tips: Look for large aggregations on goldenrod, asters, and milkweed along coastal flyways and prairie corridors. Cape May, NJ and Chincoteague, VA are famous migration bottlenecks where thousands can be seen in a single day.

animals.name: Eastern Tiger Swallowtail
animals.behavior_notes: Eastern Tiger Swallowtails are active from late spring through late summer, visiting a wide variety of flowering plants and puddling on moist soil for minerals. Males are especially visible as they patrol sunny woodland edges and hilltops.
animals.viewing_tips: Look along forest edges, near streams, and in gardens with butterfly bush, milkweed, or joe-pye weed. Mud puddles and wet sand attract puddling males in large numbers, making them easy to approach.

animals.name: Painted Lady Butterfly
animals.behavior_notes: One of the most widespread butterflies in the world, Painted Ladies undertake long-distance migrations and can appear almost anywhere during summer. They favor open fields with thistles and composite flowers for nectaring.
animals.viewing_tips: Thistle patches are the best attractant — larvae feed on thistles and adults frequently nectar there. Population sizes vary dramatically year to year depending on rainfall in their western breeding grounds, so years following wet winters in California produce spectacular migrations.

animals.name: Luna Moth
animals.behavior_notes: Luna Moths are nocturnal and are most active during warm spring nights, with adults living only about a week and not feeding at all. They are strongly attracted to lights and can often be found resting on walls or screens near bright outdoor lighting after dark.
animals.viewing_tips: Check porch lights, lit storefronts, and campground restroom exteriors on warm, calm nights in spring. Luna Moths are stunning but genuinely elusive — their short adult lifespan and nocturnal habits mean timing is key.

animals.name: Cecropia Moth
animals.behavior_notes: North America's largest native moth, the Cecropia is nocturnal and flies primarily to find mates, as adults do not feed. Females emit pheromones late at night and males can detect them from miles away, making light traps near woodland edges productive.
animals.viewing_tips: Set up a white sheet with a UV blacklight near deciduous forest edges on warm, calm spring nights. Check the sheet and surrounding vegetation every 20–30 minutes; also check outdoor lights and building walls at dawn before the sun rises.

animals.name: American Bumble Bee
animals.behavior_notes: Once one of the most common bumble bees in North America, the American Bumble Bee has suffered dramatic population declines and is now a candidate for federal endangered species listing. Workers forage actively on clover, sunflowers, and native prairie wildflowers through midsummer.
animals.viewing_tips: Visit native prairie remnants and wildflower meadows in the Great Plains, focusing on patches of clover, coneflower, and sunflower. Distinguishing this species from similar bumble bees requires close attention to yellow-and-black banding patterns — photographing for expert review is recommended.

animals.name: Firefly (Eastern)
animals.behavior_notes: Eastern Fireflies (Photinus pyralis) begin their light displays shortly after dusk, with males flying upward in a J-shaped flash pattern to attract sedentary females perched in low vegetation. Warm, humid evenings with little wind produce the most spectacular displays.
animals.viewing_tips: Find open fields or forest edges near water and arrive at dusk — displays typically last 30–90 minutes after sunset. Great Smoky Mountains NP hosts the famous synchronous firefly (Photuris carolinus) event each June, which requires a lottery permit to access.

animals.name: Periodical Cicada
animals.behavior_notes: Periodical Cicadas emerge in massive synchronized broods every 13 or 17 years when soil temperatures reach 64°F, covering trees in deafening numbers to mate, lay eggs, and die within a few weeks. The noise of a large emergence can exceed 90 decibels.
animals.viewing_tips: Check emergence maps from Cicada Safari or Brood tracker websites to know which brood is active and where. When a brood emerges in your area, simply find mature deciduous woodland — you will hear and see them without any effort.

animals.name: Dragonfly (Common Green Darner)
animals.behavior_notes: Common Green Darners are one of the few migratory dragonflies in North America, traveling in large swarms along the Atlantic coast each fall in a pattern loosely following that of Monarch Butterflies. They also breed at ponds and marshes throughout summer.
animals.viewing_tips: Visit coastal hawk-watch sites and ponds on sunny mornings after cold fronts in September–October to witness migration swarms. Hawkwatch platforms like those at Cape May Point, NJ often record thousands of migrating Green Darners on peak days.

animals.name: Praying Mantis
animals.behavior_notes: Both the native Carolina Mantis and the introduced Chinese Mantis reach adult size and are most visible in late summer and fall, when they perch prominently in meadows and gardens while hunting prey and seeking mates. Females grow largest and are easiest to spot before laying egg cases.
animals.viewing_tips: Search goldenrod, tall grasses, garden shrubs, and wildflower meadows carefully — mantises rely on camouflage and hold very still, so slow scanning is essential. Look for the distinctive triangular head and raptorial forelegs; late-season females can be 4+ inches long.

animals.name: Walking Stick
animals.behavior_notes: Walking sticks are most active at dusk and night during summer months when they feed on leaves of oak, cherry, and other deciduous trees. They remain motionless during the day, relying on their extraordinary camouflage to blend into twigs and branches.
animals.viewing_tips: Scan tree branches and shrubs slowly at eye level after sunset using a red-filtered flashlight to avoid startling them. Look for subtle movement or unusually straight 'twigs' on leafy vegetation.

animals.name: Tarantula (Desert Blonde)
animals.behavior_notes: Male Desert Blonde tarantulas emerge in large numbers in late summer and fall during their mating season, wandering open desert roads and trails in search of females. Females remain closer to their burrows but may be spotted near burrow entrances at dusk.
animals.viewing_tips: Drive desert roads slowly at dusk in September and October in southern Arizona — males are commonly seen crossing paved roads. The Saguaro National Park West district and rural roads near Tucson are particularly reliable spots.

animals.name: Black Widow Spider
animals.behavior_notes: Black widows are nocturnal hunters that build irregular, tangled webs in sheltered, dark crevices such as rock piles, hollow logs, and the undersides of park benches or outhouses. They are most active on warm nights when insect prey is abundant.
animals.viewing_tips: Use a UV flashlight at night — their silk webs fluoresce and the spiders are easier to spot near the base of rocks, woodpiles, and sheltered structures. Always use caution and keep hands away from crevices and dark gaps.

animals.name: American Horseshoe Crab
animals.behavior_notes: American horseshoe crabs mass on Delaware Bay beaches during high tides of new and full moons in May and June to spawn, with females burying eggs in the sand while smaller males cluster around them. This ancient mating ritual has occurred for hundreds of millions of years and draws large crowds of shorebirds to feed on the eggs.
animals.viewing_tips: Visit Delaware Bay beaches such as Slaughter Beach or Pickering Beach in Delaware on the high tide closest to a new or full moon in May for the most spectacular viewing. Arrive at dusk and bring a flashlight — volunteers often lead guided walks during peak spawning events.

animals.name: Giant Water Bug
animals.behavior_notes: Giant water bugs are aggressive ambush predators found in slow-moving freshwater ponds, marshes, and swamps, where they prey on tadpoles, small fish, and even small frogs. They are strong fliers and are attracted to lights at night, particularly during warm spring evenings.
animals.viewing_tips: Search shallow, still water edges in the Everglades with a flashlight after dark — giant water bugs often lurk motionless among aquatic vegetation. They also fly to artificial lights at night, so check parking area lights at trailheads for individuals that have landed nearby.

animals.name: Pacific Octopus
animals.behavior_notes: Pacific octopuses are most active during cooler months, emerging from rocky dens at dawn and dusk to hunt crustaceans and fish along shallow coastal reefs.
animals.viewing_tips: Explore tide pools and rocky intertidal zones at low tide; look for ink clouds, shed crab shells, or 'octopus gardens' of shell debris near den entrances.

animals.name: Giant Pacific Octopus
animals.behavior_notes: Giant Pacific Octopuses den in rock crevices and submarine ledges during winter, venturing out nocturnally or at twilight to ambush prey with their powerful arms.
animals.viewing_tips: Scuba diving or snorkeling in kelp forest areas near rocky reefs offers the best chance of spotting them; look for their large eyes peering from den openings.

animals.name: Bioluminescent Dinoflagellates
animals.behavior_notes: Warm summer waters fuel dinoflagellate blooms, causing waves and disturbed water to glow brilliant blue-green at night as the organisms emit light when agitated.
animals.viewing_tips: Visit calm bays or lagoons on moonless nights and gently stir the water or watch breaking waves; Mosquito Lagoon near Canaveral is a reliable hotspot.

animals.name: Jellyfish (Moon)
animals.behavior_notes: Moon jellyfish congregate in large pulsing aggregations near the surface during summer, drifting with currents and tides in sheltered bays and harbors.
animals.viewing_tips: Walk along calm harbor docks or rent a kayak to look straight down into shallow water; they are often visible from piers without any equipment.

animals.name: Dungeness Crab
animals.behavior_notes: Dungeness Crabs migrate into shallower estuaries and bays in late autumn and winter, where they are most active foraging along sandy and muddy seafloors at low tide.
animals.viewing_tips: Explore eelgrass beds and sandy tide flats at low tide during early morning; look for their distinctive broad shells half-buried in sand near the water's edge.

animals.name: American Lobster
animals.behavior_notes: American Lobsters move into shallower, warmer nearshore waters during summer to feed and molt, becoming more active and visible at dusk along rocky subtidal zones.
animals.viewing_tips: Snorkeling over rocky ledges in 10–30 feet of water at dusk is the best method; look under kelp fronds and boulder overhangs for their distinctive antennae.

animals.name: Coral (Elkhorn)
animals.behavior_notes: Elkhorn Coral spawns in late summer during brief synchronized mass spawning events triggered by warm water and lunar cycles, releasing bundles of eggs and sperm into the water column.
animals.viewing_tips: Snorkel or dive in 1–5 feet of water over reef crests; Elkhorn Coral is critically endangered so viewing is best guided by a ranger-led boat trip from Biscayne NP.

animals.name: Coral (Brain)
animals.behavior_notes: Brain Coral grows slowly in dome-shaped colonies on Caribbean reefs, extending its tentacles to feed on zooplankton primarily at night but visible as distinctive structures year-round.
animals.viewing_tips: Snorkel the Trunk Bay underwater trail or dive at Cinnamon Bay; Brain Corals are large and easy to identify by their grooved maze-like surface patterns on patch reefs.

animals.name: Sea Anemone
animals.behavior_notes: Sea Anemones extend their colorful feeding tentacles fully during calm spring conditions at low tide, anchoring to rocks in intertidal pools and filtering plankton from the water.
animals.viewing_tips: Visit tide pools at low tide during morning hours; giant green anemones are particularly visible in shaded pools at Olympic's Rialto Beach and Ruby Beach.

animals.name: Starfish (Sunflower Sea Star)
animals.behavior_notes: Sunflower Sea Stars, once the largest sea stars in the world, have been devastated by sea star wasting disease and are now critically endangered but occasionally spotted in cooler northern waters during fall.
animals.viewing_tips: This species is critically endangered and extremely rare; if spotted in a tide pool, report the sighting to park rangers or iNaturalist to aid recovery monitoring efforts.

animals.name: Pacific Sea Nettle
animals.behavior_notes: Pacific Sea Nettles aggregate in large blooms during late summer when ocean temperatures peak and upwelling brings nutrient-rich waters close to shore. They drift passively with currents, trailing long tentacles to capture zooplankton and small fish.
animals.viewing_tips: Take a boat tour or kayak around Channel Islands or Monterey Bay in summer months and scan the water surface for amber-orange bell-shaped medusae. Calm, clear days with low wind offer the best visibility into the water column.

animals.name: Mantis Shrimp
animals.behavior_notes: Mantis shrimp are most active around dawn and dusk when they emerge from burrows in sandy or rubble-strewn seafloors to hunt prey and defend territory. Spring months coincide with increased mating activity, making individuals more visible as they move between burrows.
animals.viewing_tips: Snorkel or dive in shallow reef and rubble zones at Biscayne and look carefully along the seafloor near coral rubble and sandy patches for their characteristic burrow openings. A dive light greatly improves your chances of spotting their iridescent bodies during low-light hours.
